item.description: Week 6 of the 2026 NFL season has arrived, and with it will come the first, four-team bye week of the campaign to date. The Cincinnati Bengals , Detroit Lions , Miami Dolphins and Minnesota Vikings will all get a respite in Week 6. That, plus stand-alone games on Thursday, Sunday and Monday night along with a London clash between the Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars will limit the NFL's Sunday afternoon slate to an offering of just 10 games. Per usual, Fox and CBS are set to split the rights to those 10 games. This week, it's an even 5-and-5 split, though CBS will have the right to broadcast a game in both the early- and late-afternoon windows while Fox will be limited to showing just one game per region. Later in the day, the country will be split relatively evenly, with about half seeing the Las Vegas Raiders vs. Buffalo Bills contest and half seeing the Kansas City Chiefs vs. Los Angeles Chargers game. The article on what it buys and doesn't: https://t.co/t8fuY3zHds pic.twitter.com/8GjKsAD0oj — PitByNumbers | NASCAR Data (@pitbynumbers) October 17, 2026 Racing talent is no longer the only thing a driver needs Running a competitive NASCAR program costs millions of dollars. Teams must pay for equipment, engines, engineering, transport, mechanics and countless other expenses before a driver even takes the green flag. So, Sponsorship is not an optional extra. It’s part of the business model that allows teams to compete. The problem starts when a driver’s ability to attract funding becomes a decisive factor in whether they get a seat at all. Hamlin described team owners weighing competing financial offers, with drivers potentially moving elsewhere if another candidate can bring more money to the table. He argued that the series should be built around putting its best drivers in competitive cars, rather than making funding such a significant part of the selection process. It is a difficult problem to solve. Smaller organizations cannot simply ignore sponsorship offers when their budgets depend on them. Even established teams need commercial partners to maintain their operations. But a system that rewards financial backing too heavily can create a vicious circle. A driver without substantial funding may never get the equipment needed to demonstrate their potential. And Another driver can continue racing because a sponsor is willing to support the program, even when the results are disappointing. That does not necessarily mean the funded driver lacks talent. But it does mean the opportunity to prove that talent is not distributed equally. The results show why funding alone cannot tell the whole story Statistics published by Pit by Numbers on October 16, using data through Charlotte’s 29th race of the season, provide several revealing comparisons between drivers, their sponsorship backgrounds and their results. The most useful examples are not simply the drivers with family businesses or well-known sponsors. They are the cases in which performance helps explain what a team is getting in return. Consider Brent Crews, the rookie at Joe Gibbs Racing . The figures compiled by Pit by Numbers put his average finish at 12.4, the best among the organization’s four O’Reilly Series drivers in its comparison. Crews has progressed through the racing ranks without the kind of prominent family-company sponsorship like in some other drivers’ backgrounds. He has also received backing and development opportunities, so it would be inaccurate to describe him as racing without financial support. But his results still illustrate an important point: a young driver can justify an opportunity through performance, even when their financial background is not the headline. Parker Retzlaff offers another example. According to Pit by Numbers, he averaged 12.9 in the No.99 Viking Motorsports car through Charlotte, compared with a 23.6 average finish for Matt DiBenedetto in the same entry during 2025. Retzlaff also recorded 12 top-10 finishes and four top-five results in the supplied data. A year-to-year comparison cannot account for every difference between seasons, but the improvement shows why teams should judge their investments by what happens on track as well as by the money coming in. Then there is Taylor Gray, who has family connections to the business world but has also delivered results. The supplied figures credit him with a Kansas victory, 14 top-10 finishes and 191 laps led through Charlotte. These exemples do undermine the simplistic idea that sponsorship and speed are mutually exclusive. Drivers can bring money and perform well. But the real issue is whether teams are making decisions based on the complete picture, rather than treating funding as a substitute for competitiveness. Mandatory Credit: Mike Watters-Imagn Images The contrast between Nick Sanchez’s 2025 season and Patrick Staropoli’s 2026 campaign in Big Machine Racing’s No.48 car is another example. Sanchez won at Atlanta in 2025 , led 86 laps and recorded 12 top-10 finishes in the supplied data. Staropoli , who joined the team for 2026, had yet to record a top-10 finish through the Charlotte race in the comparison. Staropoli’s car has carried SYFOVRE sponsorship. However, there is no verified evidence in the supplied material establishing that he personally paid for his seat or identifying the value of the sponsorship arrangement. A sponsor’s presence on a car does not prove that a driver bought the opportunity, and two seasons of results cannot isolate every factor affecting performance. Still, the comparison raises a legitimate question about how NASCAR teams evaluate drivers. When a car’s results change significantly from one season to the next, how much weight should be given to the driver, the equipment, the team structure and the commercial arrangement that supports the entry? There is no easy answer. But the question is worth asking when teams have limited seats and talented drivers are competing for opportunities. NASCAR’s development ladder risks becoming a financial filter Hamlin’s criticism is particularly relevant because the O’Reilly Series is an important step toward the Cup Series. It gives young drivers a chance to gain experience and show that they can handle the demands of higher-level racing. Yet if financial backing determines who gets access to competitive equipment, the development system risks filtering talent before it can be properly evaluated. The consequences extend beyond individual drivers. Fans want to see genuine competition, teams want to identify future winners, and sponsors want their investment to produce value. A system that makes it difficult to separate financial opportunity from racing merit can undermine all three goals. This is not an argument for removing sponsorship from NASCAR. That would be unrealistic. It is an argument for recognizing that the business model can influence sporting decisions, sometimes in ways that are difficult to measure. The financial pressure is not unique to NASCAR, either. Motorsport at almost every level depends on sponsorship, manufacturer support and private investment. item.title: Official | Jocelyn Blanchard leaves City Group-owned ESTAC Troyes
item.description: Official | Jocelyn Blanchard leaves City Group-owned ESTAC Troyes Jocelyn Blanchard, appointed ESTAC Troyes sporting director over the summer, has already left his role, the club have confirmed. L’ESTAC did not provide a justification for the Frenchman’s exit. Blanchard arrived three months ago. Despite the club earning promotion to Ligue 1 last season, Antoine Sibierski left the club during the interseason. Blanchard was chosen as his successor. As revealed by Romain Molina, the Frenchman was the subject of an internal enquiry. That enquiry pertained to complaints about his behaviour towards other employees at the club. Troyes already searching for Blanchard’s successor Elisa Sicking-Bressler, the head of safeguarding at the City Football Group, had travelled to the French club in order to conduct interviews regarding the complaints. In their press release, Troyes, currently second from bottom in Ligue 1 with just four points from their opening seven games, gave no reason for the sporting director’s exit. Attempts to recruit Blanchard’s successor at the Stade de l’Aube were underway. GFFN | Luke Entwistle

item.title: Kobbie Mainoo and Luke Shaw look set to miss out on Leeds United clash
item.description: Kobbie Mainoo and Luke Shaw look set to miss out on Leeds United clash Kobbie Mainoo and Luke Shaw are major doubts for Manchester United’s Premier League meeting with Leeds United today. Carrick was already managing a growing absentee list It was relayed by The Peoples Person on Saturday that Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui had not made the initial journey to Leeds. Sesko has been sidelined since suffering a shin injury against Brighton and Hove Albion in the League Cup, while Dorgu and Mazraoui sustained knocks on international duty. Mainoo and Shaw had both missed the 2-0 Champions League defeat away to Atletico Madrid. Asked about the pair before the Leeds fixture , Michael Carrick said their availability would be assessed closer to the game. It would now appear that the assessment resulted in two shakes of the head. item.title: Bucks waive Pete Nance, Johni Broome after OT preseason loss to Pacers
item.description: Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images Bucks waive Pete Nance, Johni Broome after OT preseason loss to Pacers appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Milwaukee Bucks have requested waivers on Pete Nance, Johni Broome and Jake Stephens as the team continues to reduce its roster ahead of the 2026-27 NBA regular season. The announcement came Saturday, less than 24 hours after Milwaukee suffered a 128-127 overtime loss to the Indiana Pacers in its preseason finale. Nance’s departure is the most prominent of the three moves, given his previous contributions to the Bucks. The 6-foot-9 forward/center appeared in 47 games for the Bucks last season, averaging 5.4 points and 2.7 rebounds in 15.7 minutes per contest. He shot 51.5% from the field and 42.0% from three-point range. The 26-year-old also recorded 1.0 assist per game during his previous campaign with Milwaukee. One of his best performances came in April against the Houston Rockets, when he scored 23 points and grabbed three rebounds while converting five of nine attempts from beyond the arc. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) Nance also featured in four preseason games this year, including one start, averaging 4.0 points and 3.3 rebounds in 13.0 minutes per appearance. He initially joined the Bucks on a two-way contract in February 2025 and appeared in 53 games across two seasons, posting 5.2 points, 2.6 rebounds and 1.0 assist while shooting 51.7% from the floor and 42.0% from three-point range. Although Nance’s contract did not include a guaranteed salary, Milwaukee had reportedly considered keeping him. Re-signing him to a two-way deal remains a possibility if he clears waivers, but the Bucks reportedly have concerns about another team claiming him. Broome signed with Milwaukee on October 6 after spending his rookie season with the Philadelphia 76ers as a 2025 second-round pick. He made one preseason appearance versus the Chicago Bulls on Wednesday, finishing with four points and three rebounds in nine minutes. Stephens signed with the Bucks on September 17 and played in two preseason contests. The center averaged 1.5 points and 1.0 rebound across 5.3 minutes per game. Following the moves, Milwaukee still has work to do before Monday’s deadline to finalize its regular-season roster. The team has 16 players on standard contracts and must eliminate one more standard roster spot, either by waiving a player or completing a trade that reduces its roster count. The Bucks’ overall roster currently stands at 18 players. item.title: Barcelona’s incredible attacking numbers reveal another major strength of Hansi Flick’s team
item.description: Barcelona’s incredible attacking numbers reveal another major strength of Hansi Flick’s team Barcelona’s remarkable start to the 2026-27 season has been defined by an extraordinary goalscoring record, with five goals in a match becoming the norm. Flick’s side have already scored five goals against Elche, Rayo Vallecano, Valencia, Feyenoord and Betis, while putting seven past Racing. However, the most impressive aspect is the number of different players contributing to Hansi Flick’s attacking machine. According to Mundo Deportivo , the Catalans have scored 48 goals in just 11 competitive matches, averaging 4.3 per game. Of those, 39 have come in La Liga , approximately 20 more than second-placed Atletico Madrid have scored. Barcelona now have 13 different goalscorers Saturday’s 5-2 victory over Real Betis provided another example of Barcelona’s attacking depth, with Eric Garcia, Rodri and Dani Olmo all opening their goalscoring accounts for the season. Rodri’s header from a corner was particularly special, marking his first goal since joining Barcelona. Gabriel Jesus helped Barcelona secure a victory against Real Betis. (Photo by Fran Santiago/Getty Images) Eric Garcia also found the net following Pau Cubarsi’s aerial contribution, becoming the fourth Barcelona defender to score in La Liga this season, alongside Xavi Espart, Joao Cancelo and Jules Kounde. Meanwhile, Olmo ended a frustrating 24-match wait for a goal with an outstanding finish into the far corner. Those contributions have taken Barcelona’s tally of different goalscorers to 13, matching a mark previously achieved at the start of the 1995-96 league campaign. Flick has created an attack that does not rely on one player What makes these numbers especially encouraging is that Barcelona have maintained their remarkable scoring rate even without Raphinha. Rather than relying exclusively on their forwards, Flick has built a system in which midfielders and defenders regularly arrive in dangerous positions. Hansi Flick’s Barca face a strong test against PSG. (Photo by Fran Santiago/Getty Images) The contributions from Rodri and Eric Garcia also underline Barcelona’s growing threat from set pieces, providing another way to break down opponents. When opponents concentrate on stopping Lamine Yamal or Barcelona’s other attacking stars, players such as Fermin, Olmo and Rodri tend to profit. The challenge now for Flick is to turn this attacking prowess into statement performances against PSG and Real Madrid this week. Barça are turning heads across Europe with the ease with which they are dismantling opponents. Right now, the Catalans look unstoppable, and it remains to be seen whether they can maintain this goalscoring rate against the defending European champions.

item.title: 'Bigger than football': UTSA reflects on pregame tragedy
item.description: Emergency responders tend to a service member after an accident repelling from the roof before a football game against Navy at the Alamodome, Saturday, October 17, 2026. (Cody Duty/Contributor) UTSA coach Jeff Traylor knew only that the start of the game was being delayed, so he didn't have much to share with the players. The Roadrunners returned to the locker room following pregame warmups with about 20 minutes left before kickoff, remaining unaware of the tragic scene that unfolded near midfield a few moments later. A military service member was carted from the Alamodome on a stretcher after falling from the rafters during a pregame skills demonstration. Four officers were set to rappel to the field ahead of the coin toss for UTSA's annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game Saturday against Navy, and one appeared to slide down in an uncontrolled manner, crashing to the ground. The officer was transported to an area hospital, per a UTSA spokesperson, and no further update on his condition was available Saturday night. Traylor and the Roadrunners waited in the locker room while the service member was treated by medical personnel on the field, and UTSA kicked off its 38-34 win against Navy at 7:10 p.m. - about 10 minutes later than scheduled. item.title: Breiden Fehoko accuses NFL referees for changing games despite being ‘threatened’ to lose his pension
item.description: Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images Former LSU defensive lineman Breiden Fehoko has accused NFL and college football officials of influencing game outcomes, claiming he was threatened with losing his pension after previously speaking out about officiating. Fehoko made the allegations on social media following Notre Dame’s controversial 28-24 defeat to BYU, which ended with a disputed final play that sparked fresh debate over the officials’ decisions. The former NFL player, who won a national championship with LSU in 2019, suggested that questionable officiating was not limited to one level of football. Breiden Fehoko makes serious allegations about NFL and college football referees Taking to X , Fehoko claimed that players were aware of officials allegedly manipulating games during his NFL career. He also alleged that his previous criticism of the league led to threats involving his pension. Fehoko wrote: “I won’t even be quiet about it no more. When I played in the NFL we all knew officials were rigging games certain ways. It happens at the college ranks. Last year when I put the NFL on blast about it they threatened to pull my pension. ____ em. The world deserves to know.” Fehoko played college football for LSU before beginning his professional career with the Los Angeles Chargers. He also spent time with the Pittsburgh Steelers. However, he did not identify specific officials, games or individuals allegedly involved in manipulating results. He also provided no documentation to support his claim that his pension had been threatened. The allegations therefore remain unverified, and Fehoko’s playing experience alone does not establish that either the NFL or college football games have been rigged. The timing of his comments has drawn attention to Notre Dame’s defeat to BYU, particularly the final offensive play involving wide receiver Jaden Greathouse. Notre Dame attempted a late pass towards Greathouse, but no pass interference penalty was called, prompting questions about whether the officials should have intervened. Head coach Marcus Freeman declined to criticise the referees after the game, describing the final sequence as chaotic and explaining that BYU’s defensive pressure influenced the decision to target Greathouse. While the disputed call has fuelled debate, it does not provide evidence to support Fehoko’s wider allegations. His claims about being threatened over his pension are also yet to be independently corroborated. item.title: Martinez 'back in a few weeks' after operation
item.description: Emiliano Martinez joined Chelsea this summer after six seasons at Aston Villa [Reuters] Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez says he will be fit "in a few weeks" after having an operation following the 2-0 Premier League win at Everton on Saturday. The 34-year-old Argentina international reportedly broke his jaw after a head collision with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite in the second half at Hill Dickinson Stadium. Martinez needed treatment for eight minutes before leaving the pitch on a stretcher. He was taken to hospital and manager Xabi Alonso later said he was concussed. Martinez, wearing a hospital gown, wrote on social media on ‌Sunday: "Thanks to everyone for the messages. The operation ‌went well. "The most important thing is that we won, and kept a clean sheet. In a few weeks we'll be back." Mike Penders, who replaced Martinez to make his Premier League debut, looks set to play in Chelsea's next three matches at least. They face Tottenham and Manchester United in the Premier League, with a Carabao Cup tie at Liverpool in between. Penders, 21, signed from Belgium club Genk for £17m in 2024. Alonso said: "Mike has personality. He's brave and we have full trust ‌with him. He did well when he came on. "He played in the cup games and whenever he's ⁠needed. Like the other players, whenever they are needed they can perform. "It's all about the squad - ‌that all the ​players feel important and can have ‌their moment whenever they are needed, ​and that's very positive." item.title: North London Is Red! Arsenal U18s Snatch Dramatic Late Winner Against Spurs
item.description: North London Is Red! Arsenal U18s Snatch Dramatic Late Winner Against Spurs Arsenal’s Under-18s produced a remarkable north London derby victory on Saturday, beating Tottenham 2-1 at London Colney despite losing both of their goalkeepers to injury. Mylo Bernard was the hero with two goals, including a spectacular winner in the seventh minute of stoppage time. But there was another unlikely star as Emerson Nwaneri, younger brother of Ethan, was forced to swap his outfield position for a place between the posts. And somehow, the young Gunners still managed to beat their unbeaten north London rivals! Mylo Bernard strikes twice as Arsenal fight back Tottenham arrived at London Colney sitting top of the Under-18 Premier League South and had enjoyed an impressive start to the season. They created several opportunities during the first half, but Arsenal goalkeeper Jack Talbot kept the visitors at bay. Spurs eventually broke the deadlock five minutes after the restart through Joel Vidal-Philbert, but Arsenal responded almost immediately. Bernard, who was among the young Arsenal players selected for England youth international duty , turned home Hakeem Abubakar’s delivery to level the scores just a minute later. The visitors continued to threaten, with Talbot producing an excellent save from an Armend Muslika free-kick before the game took an extraordinary turn. getty images Two injured goalkeepers and an unlikely Arsenal hero Talbot was forced off following a collision and replaced by young goalkeeper Maximillian Lo Presti. Unfortunately, Lo Presti also suffered an injury following another collision, leaving Arsenal without a recognised goalkeeper for the closing stages. Up stepped Emerson Nwaneri! The youngster, whose older brother Ethan is currently on loan at Borussia Dortmund , took the gloves as Arsenal desperately tried to hold on against their rivals. According to Tottenham’s official match report, Spurs had enjoyed plenty of opportunities throughout the match, but they could not make their advantage count. Then came an incredible finale. Deep into stoppage time, Nwaneri launched a long free-kick forward, which eventually reached Luis Muñoz. The substitute found Bernard, who cut inside and smashed an unstoppable effort in off the crossbar. Arsenal had won it in the 97th minute! The result ended Tottenham’s unbeaten start to the campaign and moved Arsenal to within three points of their rivals in the league standings. What makes this victory particularly satisfying is the character shown by the youngsters. Losing both goalkeepers could easily have ended their hopes of taking anything from the match, yet they somehow found a way to win. A north London derby victory is always worth celebrating, but this one really was something special. Could Mylo Bernard and Emerson Nwaneri be two more youngsters to keep an eye on at Arsenal? What a way to win a derby! _____________________________________________________________________________________________ ADMI

item.title: "Win Scrappy" Todd McLellan Points To Red Wings Identity
item.description: Follow Michael Whitaker On X The Detroit Red Wings bent but didn't break against the San Jose Sharks on Saturday evening, rallying from a 3-1 deficit in the third period to earn a 4-3 shootout victory at Little Caesars Arena. Emmitt Finnie and Alex DeBrincat scored third-period goals for the host Red Wings, who got the lone shootout goal from Lucas Raymond. For the Red Wings, it capped a lengthy homestand that saw them play seven of their first eight games of the season in the friendly confines of home ice; they now embark on the road for four straight contests. There was certainly room for improvement in the standings, according to head coach Todd McLellan, but he also pointed to an important benefit of playing so many games at home. "What didn't we do well enough at home? We didn't get enough points in the bank, for the amount of games we played, we'd like to have more stockpiled," he said. "But I think it allowed us to practice well. You always practice better at home...the practice time is way more valuable than it is on the road." Bookmark The Hockey News Detroit Red Wings team site to stay connected to the latest news , game-day coverage, and player features . The Red Wings now head out for a four-game Western road swing that begins on Tuesday against the Seattle Kraken, a club that beat them earlier in the month. Red Wings Complete Comeback, Defeat Sharks 4-3 Via Shootout Trailing 3-1 in the third period, the Detroit Red Wings mounted a successful comeback effort against the visiting San Jose Sharks at Little Caesars Arena. What kind of team does Detroit need to be in order to have a successful road trip? The kind of squad that wins games the hard way. "Just establishing somewhat of an identity," McLellan said of what must happen on the road. "We're going to have to be a checking team; we have to be. That's who we're going to turn into for now, and win scrappy." The Red Wings will take on the Seattle Kraken in their next game at Climate Pledge Arena on Tuesday evening. item.title: Kentucky football doesn't always win 'pretty.' But UK just keeps winning
item.description: NORMAN, OK — Before Kentucky football and Oklahoma teed it up Oct. 17, chaos was running amok throughout the SEC . Down went top-ranked Georgia. Down went fellow top-10 clubs Alabama and Texas. That havoc wasn't restricted to the conference, though. Elsewhere, two more top-five squads — Notre Dame and Indiana — suffered their first setbacks of the season. With so much upheaval across the league and national landscape, UK was sitting pretty prior to tangling with OU. But "pretty" is the last word one would use to describe Kentucky's 21-13 victory at Gaylord Family-Oklahoma Memorial Stadium. UK coach Will Stein , whose team just keeps winning and winning and winning, couldn't care less. "Somebody told me once, 'Stats are for losers,'" he said. "This is one of those games. We somehow — and I know how — found a way to win through our grit, through our toughness." So here we are, past the midpoint of the 2026 regular season, past the midpoint of October, and the Wildcats are 6-1 overall. And 4-1 in conference competition. Oh, that latter mark? It means Kentucky is tied for first place in the SEC standings alongside Georgia. A school that, obviously, needs no introduction at this point. Even in the wildest dreams of the most passionate Wildcats supporter, who ever could have imagined Kentucky would be doing this in Stein's debut season? What of Stein himself? Did he dare let himself ponder such a magical maiden campaign? Please. "I'm not really worried about where we're ranked, what our record is," he said. "It's all about, 'How can we improve?' So this was a big win on the road. Whenever you can win on the road in the SEC, it gives you a lot of confidence. ... So I'm not really worried about any standings. "I know how quickly that can turn if you don't take care of business the following week." Ironically, Kentucky's next foe is its easiest, on paper, the remainder of the regular season. item.content:encoded: NORMAN, OK — Before Kentucky football and Oklahoma teed it up Oct. 17, chaos was running amok throughout the SEC . Down went top-ranked Georgia. Down went fellow top-10 clubs Alabama and Texas. That havoc wasn't restricted to the conference, though. Elsewhere, two more top-five squads — Notre Dame and Indiana — suffered their first setbacks of the season. With so much upheaval across the league and national landscape, UK was sitting pretty prior to tangling with OU. But "pretty" is the last word one would use to describe Kentucky's 21-13 victory at Gaylord Family-Oklahoma Memorial Stadium. UK coach Will Stein , whose team just keeps winning and winning and winning, couldn't care less. "Somebody told me once, 'Stats are for losers,'" he said. "This is one of those games. We somehow — and I know how — found a way to win through our grit, through our toughness." So here we are, past the midpoint of the 2026 regular season, past the midpoint of October, and the Wildcats are 6-1 overall. And 4-1 in conference competition. Oh, that latter mark? It means Kentucky is tied for first place in the SEC standings alongside Georgia. A school that, obviously, needs no introduction at this point. Even in the wildest dreams of the most passionate Wildcats supporter, who ever could have imagined Kentucky would be doing this in Stein's debut season? What of Stein himself? Did he dare let himself ponder such a magical maiden campaign? Please. "I'm not really worried about where we're ranked, what our record is," he said. "It's all about, 'How can we improve?' So this was a big win on the road. Whenever you can win on the road in the SEC, it gives you a lot of confidence. ... So I'm not really worried about any standings. "I know how quickly that can turn if you don't take care of business the following week." Ironically, Kentucky's next foe is its easiest, on paper, the remainder of the regular season. Vanderbilt, no longer propelled by the incomparable Diego Pavia, has sunk back to the SEC cellar. It's 0-4 against league foes this fall after losing a pillow fight to Arkansas on Oct. 17. An Arkansas outfit that also was 0-fer the SEC (0-3) prior to vanquishing Vandy. It defies logic to believe the Cats could lose to the Commodores in Lexington on Oct. 24. Not with everything Kentucky has hanging in the balance. An SEC championship game appearance, which would be its first. A College Football Playoff berth, which still doesn't quite make sense to type. "Kentucky" and "College Football Playoff bid" in the same sentence? Not even a year removed from the end of the Mark Stoops tenure, which saw the program lose 13 of 16 conference contests the past two seasons? But Stoops is yesterday's news. Stein is the present. And the future. Yet for all the focus on Stein, after dispatching the Sooners, he made sure the focus wasn't on him. It was on the process. And more important, every person — big and small — who contributes to making the program better. Every day. "It's not just getting the right players, but the right people in here," he said, "with the right characteristics: grit, toughness, accountability, connection, people that are about the team. Dr. Joaquín García fell to Wellington by a 3-1 match margin at the beginning of the season, but at that point, the Bulldogs were still figuring out their identity. Thursday night proved that at some point along the way, they'd found it. García walked into Wellington's gymnasium and took down the Wolverines to win the program's fourth district title in four tries — across three different classifications. "We have a lot of seniors on the team this year," Erica Green said. "Seven girls, and one of them is a manager this year, so six players, and you know, I think they kind of rallied around them. They weren't ready for the season to end." Sophomore Daniela Leite paced the Bulldogs with 15 kills on a stellar .385 hitting percentage and 23 assists, while her freshman sister Joslyn Leite tallied 12 kills on the other side. item.title: Sheikh Jassim’s family make verbal contact with Inter Milan over major investment
item.description: Sheikh Jassim’s family make verbal contact with Inter Milan over major investment Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani’s Al Mirqab family office is said to be exploring the purchase of a minority stake in Inter, three years after his son attempted to buy Manchester United. Oaktree ownership opened the door to minority investment Oaktree Capital Management, a US investment fund management company, assumed ownership of Inter on 22 May 2024 after the club’s holding companies failed to repay a three-year loan. The Italian side subsequently strengthened their existing Qatari links by making Qatar Airways their main training-kit partner as well as their official airline partner in July 2024. Interest from Al Mirqab entered the public domain on 15 October, when Corriere della Sera identified the Qatari family office as one of several investors exploring a minority holding. It said the contacts with Oaktree were verbal and exploratory, rather than a formal negotiation. Al Mirqab had already completed a major Milan investment in April 2026, acquiring 80% of the company holding Kering’s Via Monte Napoleone 8 property. Kering received €729 million immediately, with a further €432 million deferred. Al Mirqab’s preliminary approach and Inter’s rising value Tuttosport has now provided further detail on the identity and finances of the man behind the interest. It reports that Oaktree has responded with a curt “no comment” and does not currently contemplate selling control of Inter, although it could consider an investment which leaves its majority position intact. item.title: Wigan pine for FA Cup glory as not even victory can lift them off foot of League One
item.description: Gary Caldwell, club captain in 2013 and now manager, needs much more than Saturday’s win over Reading to disperse the clouds If the 2013 FA Cup final represented a blip for the Sheikh Mansour-era Manchester City in their quest for total domination of English football, it was a historic moment for their conquerors, Wigan Athletic. Memories of that famous day at Wembley still endure for Latics’ supporters despite the relegation from the Premier League that followed. Yet watching the modern-day Wigan, who remain bottom of League One despite a 1-0 win over Reading on Saturday, makes the toppling of City in a Cup final seem an epoch ago. The club, perhaps understandably, continue to hark back to their halcyon days. Last season they brought back Gary Caldwell – club captain in 2013 – for his second stint as manager, having led the club to promotion from this division in 2015-16. Choosing to swap Exeter for a return to the Latics last season was seen as a risky move by Caldwell, considering the shoestring budget imposed upon him by Mike Danson, the owner who is keen to sell. item.description: The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically The sun shone. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free. Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.” Continue reading...

item.title: Houthi conflict casts shadow as Saudi Arabia scales back sporting pipe dreams
item.description: A match delayed by missile attack warnings is not what Cristiano Ronaldo and co signed up for but it’s the new reality; the Saudi sporting juggernaut is stalling Cristiano Ronaldo grabbed the scarf in the colours of the Saudi Arabian flag and waved it at the sparse but enthusiastic crowd, who responded with rapturous cheers. It was a gesture of defiance rather than a victory salute, encapsulating the Saudi equivalent of “Keep calm and carry on”. Monday night’s Asian Champions League Elite game between Al-Nassr and the Uzbek side Neftchi Fergana had ended with a 3-1 win for the Saudi club coached by Ange Postecoglou, with Ronaldo, supported by Sadio Mané, scoring, the smattering of star names indicative of the lure of the Saudi Pro League. Yet this isn’t quite how Ronaldo and co would have anticipated life in Riyadh. The meagre attendance aside, Monday’s game was delayed by a threat of missile attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels. A safety warning issued 15 minutes before kick-off came two days after 13 people died and more than 300 were wounded by Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport. item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! It is quite funny that PSG felt like the good guys at the Etihad Stadium but if we briefly detach ourselves from the notion that the European champions’ own sportswashing and cashsplashing has also done immeasurable damage to the beautiful game, then their 4-2 Bigger Cup shellacking of Manchester City was pure cinema, baby! I was stunned at reading the comments in support of Manchester City keeping their trophies, coming out of the mouth of their Bigger Cup rivals at PSG (yesterday’s Quote of the Day). Given the example of the organisers of the Tour de Lance … sorry, the Tour de France, this kind of ‘keep the awards you won’ stuff might get him sent to the Bastille. Or consider Formula One. They’ve got all kinds of rules about driver behaviour on the racetrack, and additional rules about what the crew can and cannot do to your car. Cars get inspected before each race, and there are also mandatory post-race inspections for every car. You might drive your car first across the line to the cheers of the crowd, but if the post-race inspection discovered that you cheated in how your team designed your vehicle, your memory of crossing the line is all you get to keep. Think about that for a minute. If the Premier League and Fifa cannot clear the bar for morals in sport set by the UCI and FIA, that says a lot. And none of it good” – Peter Rehwaldt. My friend Bernard grew up in Coventry. And as a boy he thought the team was called ‘Coventry City Nil’. I would get out more, but I’m a Manchester United fan” – Brendan Hughes. item.description: Former Manchester City player is coming out of retirement at 40 to play one match for ambitious Supreme Sha Tin Hong Kong, China (as is the official football name), has long tried to follow the advice of Han Solo in Return of the Jedi: keeping their distance from China while trying not to look like they are keeping their distance. It is all about maintaining an independent football association and the trappings and privilege that come with it. There was some talk a few years ago about getting a Hong Kong team in the Chinese Super League, when the spending was in full flow, and although that did not happen the local Premier League has belatedly got in on the act – kind of. This glittering city is not known as a football hotbed but has a long history in the sport that started when it was a British colony and has continued since it became a special administrative region of China in 1997. George Best, Peter Shilton, Arie Haan, Bobby Moore, Diego Forlán, Nicky Butt, René van de Kerkhof, Tony Morley, Gordon McQueen and Craig Foster have played in the territory and soon David Silva will too. item.description: It’s not just that the club’s recent charges themselves are unprecedented – it’s the language used to describe them too Sign up for our free newsletter here The language of football is a fine and highly nuanced dialect. Minor deviations from the familiar, almost imperceptible to outsiders, can set off alarm bells: what’s really going on there? Why isn’t he happy? What’s she hinting at? item.description: Manchester City unrepentant in victory, Spurs make progress of a sort and Noni Madueke meets the moment The manner of Manchester City’s victory at Liverpool was an article of both vindication and vilification. Those gleefully wielding inflatable bananas in the Anfield away end could thumb their noses. Why not enjoy the dances of defiance until the music stops? The same went for City players, asked to perform under the darkest of clouds, able to focus, at last, on football, rather than legal argument and uncertain futures. Beyond City, the sight of a club found guilty of 100-plus charges laying waste to such rivals as Liverpool was deeply uncomfortable . The Premier League season and product are badly damaged until the matter is somehow resolved. What happened at Anfield should double the haste for a resolution. Chants of “cheat” whenever City players, the game already won, slipped the ball around, are bound to be repeated at other stadiums. Enzo Maresca has described his club’s plight as “noise” but his team’s victory did absolutely nothing to turn the volume down. item.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game. What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it was perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “ spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales. Continue reading...

item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
